7.7.m: Glorious Vyāsa said: / Again I shall proclaim the supreme glorification of the Gaṅgā, / hearing which all men may obtain all desires.
One who has not performed a bath in the Gaṅgā, the mother of the world— / upon seeing his face, one must immediately look upon the sun.
Whoever remembers with devotion the two syllables ‘Gaṅ-gā’ at dawn, / his sins perish, like darkness at the rising of the dawn.
By whom the daughter of Jahnu, the best of rivers, has not been seen, / all his food, water, and other [offerings] are unacceptable.
Abandoning the bodies of those who bathe in the Gaṅgā, / sins enter the limbs of those who do not bathe in the Gaṅgā.
Oh, wonder! Oh, wonder! And oh, what a wonder this is: / fools fall into hell while the name of the Gaṅgā exists!
Whoever carries even a drop of Gaṅgā water on his head with devotion, / that twice-born is released from great sins, such as the murder of a brahmin.
On whose forehead the excellent sand of the Gaṅgā is seen, / that virtuous person purifies the entire world; there is no doubt here.
Whoever looks with supreme reverence upon one coming from the bank of the Gaṅgā, / that person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices.
Whoever says, “I am going to the bank of the Gaṅgā; come along,” / to him Viṣṇu, pleased in spirit, grants all desires.
Recalling the name ‘Gaṅgā’, even if a person bathes / in well-water, he will obtain the fruit of a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Whoever receives a drop of Gaṅgā water measuring [no more than] a mustard seed / at the time of death, he would go to the supreme abode.
Right on this subject, hear, O brahmin seer, an ancient legendary history, / by the mere hearing of which the goddess Gaṅgā is pleased.
In the Tretā age there was a righteous brahmin named Dharmasva, / tranquil, restrained, endowed with compassion, master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas,
truth-speaking, free from anger, free from violence, with subdued senses, / desiring the welfare of all beings, and always devoted to the practice of yoga.
To cross over the ocean of cyclic existence, that brahmin, a Vaiṣṇava man, / worshipped Keśava, the lord of the gods, with practical yoga.
Once, having reached an auspicious day, that twice-born, a bull among brahmins, / a seeker of liberation, went to the bank of the Jāhnavī for the purpose of bathing.
Having bathed there in the waters of the Gaṅgā and performed water-oblations and other rites, / carrying a vessel with Gaṅgā water, he set his mind on going home.
At that time, O twice-born, a vaiśya named Ratnākara, / having conducted trade, was returning, surrounded by all his servants.
One servant of his, known as Kālakalpa, / with a staff in hand, having committed every sin, approached, O brahmin.
Then, exhausted by the weariness of the road, an ox belonging to that Ratnākara / fell asleep on the road, O best of brahmins.
Seeing that bull sleeping on the road, Kālakalpa then / beat it many times with a staff, exceedingly pitiless.
Arising in anger caused by the blows of that staff, / he was gored by the bull with its two exceedingly sharp horns.
His chest pierced by the two horns, his eyes rolled back, / Dharmasva, full of compassion, quickly went near him.
Then, taking an excellent tulasī leaf from his ear, / he was sprinkled with divine drops of Gaṅgā water by that wise man.
Beholding that life had departed, that brahmin, who knew the supreme truth, / was astonished and set his mind on going to his own home, O best of the twice-born.
Then, while walking on the road, reciting the names of the Gaṅgā, the wise man / saw the messengers of Yama ahead by thousands of crores upon crores.
Some had one foot severed, and some had one hand severed; / some had their ears severed, and some had only one eye.
Some had their noses severed, and some had their tongues severed; / some had broken teeth, and some were deprived of teeth.
Some had their entire bodies smeared with streams of blood; / some had dishevelled hair, and some were deprived of mouths.
Some were likewise naked, and some had their chests shattered; / and some had their limbs mangled by exceedingly sharp arrows.
Others had their hands and fingers bound with firm ropes, / crying out in pain, and some were intent on fleeing.
Seeing the servants of Yama in such a state, that best of the twice-born, / his heart trembling with fear, thereupon became completely frozen.
Then, summoning his courage, that brāhmaṇa, a devotee of Hari, / asked Yama’s servants, [who looked like] Kirātas, in sweet words:
Dharma said: / 'Who are you, deformed in appearance, holding nooses and clubs in your hands, / with faces terrifying with fangs, and shining like burning coals?
You are all mighty heroes, with eyes like blazing fire; / yet by whom has this misfortune been inflicted upon you?'
Yama's messengers said: / 'We are all messengers of Yama, ever executing Yama's commands. / O brāhmaṇa, this staff of ours has experienced a very great disaster.'
Dharmasva said: / 'You arrived suddenly, possessing great strength and valor; / by whom or how has this misfortune been inflicted to such an extent?'
Yama's messengers said: / 'Cast off fear, best of brāhmaṇas, and listen to the entire account / of how this extremely unbearable sorrow befell us.
He who was torn apart with horns by a bull, like Death himself— / we, servants, were dispatched by Dharmarāja to fetch him.
Commanded by him, all of us, weapons in hand, / arrived here to bind that foremost of sinners and lead him away.
Then, having reached his time, that evil-minded one, like Death himself, / was torn apart by the bull's horns, which served as the instrument.
Then, out of compassion, by one chanting the names of Gaṅgā, / that foremost of sinners was sprinkled there with drops of Gaṅgā water.
Although he was freed from sin by the sprinkling of drops of Gaṅgā water, / [we] made an effort to bind him tightly with ropes and take him away.
To take him away as well, the Lord of gods, the protector of those seeking refuge, / sent his own messengers of great strength and valor.
Certain messengers arrived then by Nārāyaṇa's command, / and in anger they said this to us on the path, O best of brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu's messengers said: / "Who are you, illustrious ones? Why do you bind this noble-minded soul with a noose / and lead him away? Whose servants are you?
Leaving this great soul, flee at your ease; / otherwise we will cut off your heads with the edge of the discus!"
Having heard these proud words of the messengers of Acyuta, / O best of brāhmaṇas, they were answered back by us:
"We are all the messengers of the staff-bearer, the ruler of life; / having taken this foremost of sinners, we are going to Śamana’s abode.
You are all noble-souled, adorned with garlands of tulasī, / with eyes like blossomed lotus petals, mighty, and bearing Garuḍa on your banners.
You wear divine garments, are handsome as the throat of a peacock, / four-armed, and holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Who are all of you, endowed with such attributes and all auspicious marks? / And why do you wish to lead away this foremost of sinners?"
Viṣṇu's messengers said: / "We are all messengers of Viṣṇu; we have arrived here / to take this meritorious man at once to Vaikuṇṭha.
Release swiftly this devotee of the blessed Lord, his own kin, freed from sin, / O servants of Yama, if you wish to live!"
Having heard this pervasive statement of theirs again, O brāhmaṇa, / listen to what was said by us in anger; it is now told:
"This sinner is of evil conduct, the committer of a thousand murders of brāhmaṇas, / ungrateful, a cow-killer, a slayer of friends, and wicked-minded.
Immense amounts of gold, measuring like Mount Meru, were stolen by him, / and the wives of others were constantly abducted by this vile soul.
Thousands of crores of living beings, O servants of Viṣṇu, / were killed by him in many ways, and women were murdered as well.
He committed misappropriation of deposits, incest with his own mother, / and the eating of cow's flesh day after day.
Violence to others was committed by him, and the burning of others' houses, / slandering others in assemblies, and the abortion of a widow's fetus.
A guest arriving at his house he slaughtered at night with sharp swords / out of greed for wealth, O best one, like a Yavana.
These and other sins, great and countless, / this vile and foolish man committed, and not the least bit of auspicious deed.
Therefore, this great sinner is being led to the house of torment; / for sinners are to be punished by Dharmarāja, O excellent ones.
If you are indeed the messengers of the God of gods, the Lord, / then why do you wish to take this foremost of sinners?"
Viṣṇu's messengers said: / "What you have said is indeed true; there is no doubt about this: / sinners are always to be punished by the ruler of life.
Yet this man is completely freed from sin by being sprinkled with drops of Gaṅgā water; / therefore, we will all lead him to Hari's abode.
Sins remain in the bodies of embodied beings only so long / as drops of Gaṅgā water, which are very hard to attain, do not touch them.
Just as all darkness is destroyed by a single digit of the moon, / so is sin destroyed even by a single drop of Gaṅgā water.
A sinner is freed from sin by merely remembering the names of Gaṅgā; / what wonder is there that he is freed upon directly beholding her water?
Though cool, Gaṅgā water acts like fire in the forest of sin, / just as cold water acts like burning fire in a lotus bed.
Therefore, this man of virtuous deeds is a second Keśava himself; / depart, servants of Śamana, if you desire welfare!"
Hearing this speech of those messengers of Keśava, / listen to what was then spoken by us again, laughing aloud:
"Oh, what a wonder! Oh, what a wonder! This abode of sin / is freed from all sins merely by the sprinkling of Gaṅgā water!
Action acquired by one's own hand, whether good or evil, / cannot be shed by a mortal without experiencing it, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
We have all arrived to take him away by Yama's order; / at whose word should this foremost among sinners be abandoned by us?"
Viṣṇu's messengers said: / "You are indeed of sinful intellect, devoid of discernment, / because the virtues of the daughter of Jahnu are not known by you.
Action prohibited in the Veda is considered sin; / that action which is approved by the Veda is alone called righteous.
We have heard that Lord Nārāyaṇa himself is the self-existent one; / as is Viṣṇu, so is Gaṅgā, and Gaṅgā alone destroys all sin.
Whether an action fashioned by one's own hands is evil or good, Hari [settles it]; / when Hari is pleased, where can the sins of embodied beings remain?
You have reached this state through sins accumulated in other births; / why, even today, being evil-doers, do you desire sin?
You revile Gaṅgā, and you revile Viṣṇu as well; / therefore, we will slay you sinners with the edge of the discus!"
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Viṣṇu, their eyes red with wrath, / began a battle with us, O best of the virtuous.
"Let the messengers of the ruler of living beings be slain!" they cried in rage, / and uttering this repeatedly, they struck us with the edge of the discus.
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Viṣṇu, exceedingly fierce in battle, / all blew their conches at once, their minds joyful.
Then, like the rumbling of rain clouds, our lion-roars / and the stretching of our bows pervaded the three worlds, O brāhmaṇa.
Then with trees, stones, and showers of mountain [peaks], / as well as arrows, those messengers of Viṣṇu were shattered by us.
With spears and bhindipālas, with arrows and clubs, / with axes, knives, staves, and spikes,
and with swords, lances, and sharp arrows, / with maces, the edges of discs, and terrifying iron shafts,
with these and other terrible weapons, those servants of Viṣṇu / struck repeatedly in rage, like thunderbolts upon the great ocean.
Shattered by their weapons, we all fled in terror; / some fell in battle by the thousands, their life-breaths gone.
Then, seeing that we were devoted to fleeing, / those mighty servants of Viṣṇu blew their conches with joy.
Then, having severed the bonds of Kālakalpa, O best of the twice-born, / they placed him on an aerial car and went to the city of the Lord.
By the power alone of being sprinkled with spray from the Gaṅgā, O best of beings, / even the great sinner Kālakalpa attained the same world as Hari.
Having stayed there for a hundred kalpas, enjoying delightful pleasures, / and having attained knowledge right there, he reached supreme liberation.
Through the powers of the Gaṅgā, our misery has departed, O lord. / Go, O brāhmaṇa, may good betide you; return well-pleased to your own home.”
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Yama went to the city of Yama, O twice-born; / and again, he whose wealth was virtue, being pleased, went to the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, the mother of all the worlds, / with folded hands that vipra praised the supreme sovereign:

Dharmasva said: / “O Gaṅgā, mother of the entire universe, whose waves ripple, / who are a garland of flowers on the most lovely head of the Sinless One, / who remove the dust from both charming feet of the enemy of Kaṃsa, / with devotion I bow to you who bring about the destruction of sins.

O mother, giver of all happiness, supreme boat for the wretched, / whose host of qualities is sung by multitudes of vipras such as Vyāsa, rich in virtues, / a boat in the midst of the terrifying great ocean of saṃsāra, / I revere your pair of feet, which take away sins.

Even by a drop of whose water, O daughter of Jahnu, the king named Saudāsa, / though guilty of killing ten million twice-born men, / obtained liberation unattainable even by the gods of heaven— / to that you I bow with my head; O giver of boons, be gracious!

While I utter your names—Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta, Janārdana, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Gaṅgā— / O goddess, O mother, dispeller of the sins of saṃsāra, / may the fall of my body take place in your water here, through your grace.

What use are austerities, O sovereign of all, what use are prayers, / what use are gifts, or sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice? / Having received a spray of your water, human beings, / even great sinners, go to liberation unattainable by the gods.

You alone are Svāhā, O supreme sovereign, you are Svadhā / for the complete satisfaction of the hosts of gods and the world of the ancestors; / you whose nature consists of the three qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, / who bring about creation, maintenance, and dissolution—to that you I offer praise.

Whoever always bears upon the surface of their forehead the sand / and mark [made] with the mud of your bank, O goddess, / and speaks with devotion your name, the abode of all rasas— / may every speck of dust from your feet be upon my head in just this way.

Having made a dwelling on your bank, O Tripathagā, / having drunk your water that destroys sins, / remembering your name and gazing upon the delight of your waves, / O destroyer of the bonds of saṃsāra, may my birth ever take place!

Thinking the path to heaven to be extremely impassable, O auspicious one, / men, though exalted, become frightened; / but in vain, surely, because your nectar-granting water / has become a stairway for the journey to heaven.

Sins and hordes of diseases remain in the body, O sovereign of all, / giver of worldly enjoyment, only as long / as men do not take a bath in your spotless waters, / O Tripathagā, foremost among rivers.

To the further shore of whose greatness even Acyuta, Virañci, Śiva, and the others, / as well as the host of gods led by Śakra, cannot go, / you who bestow the state of supreme liberation— / to that you, some, through delusion, refer merely as a river.

7.7.m:
O Gaṅgā, giver of all happiness, only a fraction / of your greatness does the blessed Paśupati know, / since that foremost among the gods, with utmost devotion, / always carries you, the sovereign of the universe, on his head.

O Gaṅgā, O goddess, mother of the universe, be gracious, O supreme sovereign! / Protect me, praise be to you; protect me, your own servant.

You whose nature is the supreme Brahman, the sole mother of all the worlds— / am I, with a bewildered mind here, able to praise you, O giver of liberation?”

Vyāsa said: / Praised thus by that wise vipra, / the Gaṅgā, the sustainer of the world, suddenly appeared embodied, O twice-born.

He saw the Gaṅgā before him, two-armed, seated upon a makara, / white as a jasmine, the moon, and a conch, adorned with all ornaments.

Seeing the Gaṅgā before him, chanting “Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,” / he bowed to her feet, embracing the earth with his head.

Enchanting him with smiling glances, highly pleased, the supreme sovereign / then said to that vipra: “Choose a boon, O Jaimini.”
Dharmasva said: / “O mother, from the touch of your water even a slayer of a brāhmaṇa attains liberation; / by me you are seen in person—what else is there for me to accomplish?
Nevertheless, I ask for one boon: in your water, O supreme sovereign, / may my death occur, O goddess, while remembering your name.
Whoever praises you with the hymn composed by me, O eternal sovereign, / having enjoyed all desires, shall also go to the good destination at the end.”
Gaṅgā said: / “I am pleased with this devotion of yours, O best of the twice-born. / Soon, all welfare will be yours; there is no doubt.
Whatever man recites this hymn composed by you at the three twilights, / to him also, well-pleased, I shall grant excellent liberation.”
Vyāsa said: / Having granted this boon to him, to the vipra named Dharmasva, / that goddess, tender to her devotees, vanished right there, O best of vipras.
And having obtained the boon, that vipra became one who had achieved his purpose; / he remained right there on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā, O vipra.
Then, after a long time, in the spotless waters of the Jāhnavī, / having attained an easy death, he went to the supreme abode.
Even the evil-minded Kālakalpa, sprinkled with the spray of Gaṅgā's water, / attained supreme liberation; what need be said of others, O twice-born?
Even touching the water of the Gaṅgā unintentionally brings about results; / what might happen for those who touch it with devotional disposition, I indeed cannot fathom.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā—this is declared by me again and again— / by touching a drop of whose water the supreme abode is attained.
Those who, with devotional disposition, touch even a drop of the water of the best of rivers here, / surely go to the abode of Acyuta, completely freed from all terrible sins.

7.8.m: Vyāsa said: / Again I shall speak of the excellent glorification of the Gaṅgā, O best of vipras; / drink the nectar of the tale of the Gaṅgā if you desire liberation.
All gifts have been given by him, all sacrifices have been performed by him, / Viṣṇu has been thoroughly worshipped by him whose devotion is in the mother of Bhīṣma.
Whatever acts of dharma are performed in the Gaṅgā, / all of them become imperishable for him, O Jaimini.
Whoever, seeing water carrying the waters of the Gaṅgā, / rises and approaches it with devotion, becomes one who has performed a thousand horse sacrifices.

Whoever does not stand up in devotion when the waters of the Gaṅgā arrive,
O Jaimini, his state as a beast is everlasting, birth after birth.

Having approached the water of the Gaṅgā, he who does not receive it with devotion—
his merit accumulated across tens of millions of births is destroyed in an instant.

A person who turns away someone desiring to go to the bank of the Gaṅgā, O twice-born one,
shall go, together with a crore of his family lineages, to the Raurava hell.

He who discharges urine or feces on the bank of the Gaṅgā—
no expiation is seen for him even through hundreds of crores of kalpas.

He who deposits phlegm, spittle, eye-discharge, tears, or excrement
on the bank of the Gaṅgā shall certainly become a denizen of hell.

And he who casts food-scraps or mucus directly into the water of the Gaṅgā
goes to a terrible hell and incurs the sin of killing a brahmin.

The foolish man who commits a sin upon the bank of the Gaṅgā—
that sin indeed becomes imperishable; it is not quieted at other holy places.

A sin committed at another holy place is destroyed in the Gaṅgā;
but a sin that is committed in the Gaṅgā is not quieted anywhere.

Therefore, sin must not be committed at the Gaṅgā by those learned in the scriptures;
by deed, mind, and speech, an accumulation of righteousness should be gathered.

Those are not true lands, those are not mountains, nor are those forests,
where the river of the gods, the destroyer of sins, does not abide.

Even for a moment, O Jaimini, having left the bank of the Gaṅgā,
one should not reside elsewhere, even if there are hundreds of duties.

Even eating the food of alms, one should dwell on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
and not elsewhere even for a moment, even having attained kingship over the earth.

Casting off the body in the Gaṅgā, even a killer of a brahmin is liberated;
elsewhere, even a performer of a thousand horse sacrifices might not attain liberation.

Dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he who is devoted to the worship of Hari—
he by whom Hari was never worshipped in other births—

devotion arises for him toward the Gaṅgā, the mother of the world.
Let all men listen! Again and again I proclaim:

Having performed a bath in the Gaṅgā, let the supreme abode be attained!
The mortal who at the time of death recites, ‘Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,’

freed from all sins, rejoices in heaven for ten thousand yugas.
He in whom the beginning of an account of the Gaṅgā arises at the time of death, O twice-born one,

he, with all blemishes dissolved, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, the wise one who remembers at the time of death, O best of the twice-born,

the liberation-granting name ‘Gaṅgā’, Hari becomes pleased with him.
He who, at the time of death, has the excellent sectarian mark made of Gaṅgā-clay,

and casts off his body beholding one who is bathing in the Gaṅgā—
even at a cremation ground, O best of the twice-born, he obtains death in the Gaṅgā.

For as long as a person's bones remain in the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of kalpas he is magnified in the world of Viṣṇu.

The wise person whose ashes, bones, fingernails, and hair
sink into the Gaṅgā, he shall reside in the abode of Viṣṇu.

What result a man obtains when his bones are resting in the Gaṅgā,
all that result I will declare; listen with undistracted mind, O twice-born one:

Once upon a time, the blessed Śakra, adorned with manifold ornaments,
went passionately to his pleasure-house with the young woman Padmagandhā.

She, Padmagandhā, connoisseur of pleasures, having attained fresh youth,
pleased the god by presenting various delightful flavors.

On the golden couch of that rival wife, the fawn-eyed maiden,
Jiṣṇu, delighted and infatuated by the god of love, sat at her feet.

Then Śakra himself, having prepared a golden betel roll,
gave it to her, exceedingly pleased, his mind captivated by her virtues.

At that very time, Paulomī, the foremost of beauties,
adorned with every ornament, came in person to that chamber.

Seeing Śakra in such a state—the lord and sovereign over all the gods—
Paulomī, endowed with auspicious marks, became very angry and spoke:

All the thirty gods touch your feet with their heads;
how is it, O lord, that you are at the feet of Padmagandhā, a maidservant?

Because of fragrance the bee may be courted, but it does not win that renown.
You are the lord of ten million beauties, knowing all sentiments, O master;

how can you commit such an exceedingly base act?
O Padmagandhā, devoid of good qualities, O maidservant, go far away!

You are the mistress upon the couch, and Śakra is at your feet!
Vyāsa said:
Then, having been repeatedly scolded by that Paulomī, the chaste Padmagandhā,

that noble woman spoke out of anger.
Padmagandhā said:
My master himself knows my virtue and my fault.

By what authority have you come and reviled me, O virtue-less one?
Others perceive virtues and faults even with two eyes;

O evil-minded one, would he not perceive them even with a thousand eyes?
Just as people's faults spread abroad, their virtues do not likewise.

First the stain of the moon is seen by discerning people.
[If I am] an idle speaker, cruel, misshapen, and devoid of virtues,

when I have no virtues, then let your husband attend to you!
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Padmagandhā, with lotus-red eyes out of anger,

stood up from the golden couch, uttering a great lament.
Indra said:
O beloved, mistress of my life, foremost lady, having left me, where are you going?

What offense have I committed against you? Tell me that, O beautiful woman!
O beloved, I am truly your slave; I perform the duty of a slave for you.

A maidservant becomes a slave's wife; whose words do you listen to?
Rising then, Śakra, his mind agitated by infatuation for her,

seated that foremost beauty upon his lap once again.
Śacī said:
O Krauñcī, blessed is your life; my life is certainly useless!

You are always fortunate in your husband; I, an excellent lady, am unfortunate.
As long as your merit is not exhausted, O Krauñcī, [you will enjoy; but] that merit will reach exhaustion.

Born in the race of curlews, you will experience sorrow again!
Meanwhile, sport at ease with the king of the gods as you please.

After some days, O Krauñcī, this will not belong to you, O worthless one!
Hearing those most wonderful words of hers, Padmagandhā,

casting aside hostility, bowed and said to the virtuous lady.
Padmagandhā said:
O daughter of Puloman, O woman of beautiful hips, strange is this that you have spoken!

How am I a curlew? Tell me, I wish to hear carefully:
Who was I, where did I live, and how, being chaste, did I come here?

In how much time will my merit reach exhaustion?
Śacī said:
O Padmagandhā, formerly you were indeed born as a curlew bird,

living on the earth, eating impure carrion and worms.
There is a certain banyan tree on the charming bank of the Gaṅgā;

having fashioned a nest there, you made your dwelling.
Once, upon that banyan tree, by a black serpent

entering your nest, you were bitten and suddenly met your death.
All your flesh that serpent devoured in anger.

Your bones, stripped of flesh, remained right there, O fair-faced one.
Eventually, O blessed lady, that [tree] was toppled by great winds;

broken, it fell into the Gaṅgā together with its roots, O noble woman.
When that banyan tree had fallen into the Gaṅgā,
Those bones of yours were inundated by the waters of the Gaṅgā, O noble lady; / as long as those bones remain in the Gaṅgā,
so long will you always be fortunate in [the love of] your lord. / Thus all this has now been told to you by me, O Padmagandhā,
by the power of which merit even Śakra is subject to your control. / Blessed indeed is the goddess Jāhnavī, by whose favor, O curlew-bird,
you, [though once] untouchable by Cāṇḍālas, now sleep on the lap of the thunderbolt-wielder [Indra]!’ / Humiliated by him, the virtuous Pulomajā,
her lotus-face faded, went away as she had come. / But that fair lady Padmagandhā remained right on Śakra’s lap.
That utterance remained as if awakened in her heart. / Then once, O twice-born, the lord of the gods, well-pleased by her virtues,
himself said to her, ‘Choose a boon, O woman of shapely hips!’ / Padmagandhā said: / ‘You are the lord of all the gods and the master of ten million women;
yet you are subservient to me, my lord; what need is there for other boons? / Even so, if indeed you wish to grant a boon, O best of the gods,
make a solemn vow before me in deed, mind, and speech.’ / Indra said: / ‘[My] life, wealth, kingdom, and attendants—
command me: which of these indeed shall I give to you, O lovely lady? / Truly, truly, again truly; of this there is no doubt:
whatever you wish, O fawn-eyed lady, that I will surely give you.’ / Padmagandhā said: / ‘If indeed you are pleased, O lord of the thirty [gods],
grant me this boon: let me be born again in the womb of an elephant.’ / Indra said: / ‘I have made a pledge, O woman of shapely hips; I will indeed give you the boon.
Yet many sorrows have entered into my heart. / Without seeing you, O woman of lovely limbs, not a moment's joy is found.
How can I bear the unbearable, long separation from you? / If you have compassion for me, O lady of full breasts,
then remain with me for some days, O fair-bodied woman!’ / Thereupon, speaking of the great wealth of the supreme king of the gods,
that chaste lady dwelt for ten thousand years in the abode of the gods. / Padmagandhā said: / ‘Give [your] permission, O lord of the gods, so that I may accomplish my cherished desire.
I shall go to the realm of action; I salute your two feet.’ / Indra said: / ‘Measuring the ocean of your love with me, O moon-faced lady,
stay for a few days; thereafter you may go as you please.’ / Then in the chamber of delights, day and night with him,
that Padmagandhā, sporting, dwelt for thirty thousand years. / Then, full of joy, she said to the lord of the gods:
‘Give the command: I shall depart for the earth now.’ / Indra said: / ‘Cast off this stupor, O woman of shapely hips; remain right here with me!
I cannot abandon you, who are dearer to me than my very life-breaths.’ / Padmagandhā said: / ‘When my merit is exhausted, O lord of the gods, and I must go to earth,
then there will be a long separation between you and me. / Since in that separation, O lord, I must go to earth again,
I wish to attain heaven again for the purpose of acquiring merit. / Having gone to the realm of action, by whatever means, O Vāsava,
I shall act so that there will never be separation from you.’ / Indra said: / ‘O gentle lady, since this action is truly desired by you,
then go; you will quickly return again, O beautiful one!’ / Then, his body soaked with tears flowing from both his eyes,
embracing her with both arms, Śakra said, ‘Go, O beloved!’ / Then, by his command, the virtuous lady came to the realm of action.
She was born in the womb of a cow-elephant, remembering her past birth, O twice-born. / Remembering her own story, she, after some days,
born well from the elephant womb, went to the bank of the Jāhnavī. / Having attained a bath in the Gaṅgā, adorned with the mud of the Gaṅgā,
calling out ‘Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā!’, she entered a deep pool. / Having gone into that pool of the Gaṅgā, the cow-elephant, resembling a mountain,
remembering her own birth, met her demise again. / Beholding the daring of that cow-elephant, all the deities
joyfully showered her with superior flowers, such as the pārijāta. / Then Śakra, surrounded by all the hosts of gods, to bring her back,
went swiftly with a glad mind to the dark-limbed lady, after their long separation. / Seeing her in the Puṣpaka aerial car, possessed of a divine body, the lord of the gods,
recounting his sorrows, departed to his own abode. / Pulomajā, Rambhā, Pramlocā, and Urvaśī,
and other lovely young women, abandoning [their pride], came with joy before her. / Spreading joy in the heart of Śakra, that fair woman,
fortunate and beloved with affection, dwelt in the city of Puraṃdara. / As long as her bones remain in the Gaṅgā, O Jaimini,
for so long a hundred crores of families have their abode in the dwelling of the gods. / Whatever kings existed on earth in royal realms through the power of asceticism,
she becomes the object of love for all of them, an immortal beauty. / Such is the fruit, O Jaimini, from the immersion of bones in the Gaṅgā alone;
it is impossible to state the fruit for one who abandons the body in the Gaṅgā. / As long as a dead body's bones remain in the Gaṅgā, O Jaimini,
for a hundred crores of kalpas its residence is in the abode of the gods. / When a dead body is seen in the Gaṅgā carried by the currents, O twice-born,
hear the fruit of that embodied soul, O Jaimini: / in heaven, fanned by the breeze of lovely chowries shaken by divine maidens,
he rests asleep on a golden couch, delighting in pleasure. / One whose dead body is seen on the sands of the Jāhnavī,
heated by the rays of the sun, I tell of his family: / his entire body smeared with fragrant, divine sandalwood pastes,
accompanied by divine women, he sports in heaven forever. / Hear the fruit for one whose body is seen torn apart in the mother of Bhīṣma [the Gaṅgā]
by crows, vultures, herons, and birds: / in heaven, his chest embraced by the plump, high, and charming breasts of divine maidens,
he sleeps continuously on a couch. / And one whose fallen bones are seen in the Gaṅgā,
surrounded by ants, worms, and flies— / hear from me, O Brahmin, as I tell of his imperishable reward:
the dust of his feet wiped away by the crown ornaments on the heads of bowing hosts of the thirty gods, / he acts as Indra in heaven for a long time.
Even if the falling of one's body should occur in the Gaṅgā involuntarily, / that person, liberated from all sins, becomes Nārāyaṇa.
And one whose coals [of the funeral pyre] are seen moving in the Gaṅgā by the waters, / he will dwell in heaven for more than a hundred kalpas, equal in number to the coals.
The end of all other merits is seen eventually, / but when the body has fallen into the Gaṅgā, there is no exhaustion of merit.
What is the use of saying much here? What is certain is now told: / the glory of one whose body is surrendered in the Gaṅgā is simply unknowable.

A devout mortal in this world who, with devotional feelings, ever touches the Gaṅgā's water that destroys multitudes of terrible sins, / having crossed over the dreadful water of the ocean of worldly existence, reaches the other shore by the boat of boundless contentment.'

7.9.m: Jaimini said: / ‘Tell further, O teacher, of the supreme glorification of the Gaṅgā; / on account of its sweetness, drinking the nectar of the stories of the Gaṅgā is desired once again.’

Vyāsa said:
Even so, I will tell you, since you are a devotee of the Gaṅgā. / Fruitful are the two feet of men that go to the bank of the Jāhnavī;
and fruitful are the two ears that hear the sound of the Gaṅgā's waves. / And that tongue is fruitful which knows the difference of taste in its water;
and fruitful are those eyes in beholding the lovely ripples of the Jāhnavī. / That is declared to be a forehead which bears the clay-mark of the Gaṅgā;
and those hands are fruitful that are devoted to worshipping Hari on the bank of the Jāhnavī. / And fruitful is that body, O best of the twice-born,
which has fallen into the spotless water of the Jāhnavī, yielding the fruit of the four aims of life. / All the ancestors dwelling in heaven, seeing [him] going to the bank of the Jāhnavī,
rejoice, praise [him], and say, O Jaimini: / “The merit that we performed formerly for the attainment of a good destiny
shall become inexhaustible, since such a son has been born. / By him we are now satisfied with the waters of the Gaṅgā;
we shall go to the supreme abode, which is difficult to attain even for the gods. / Whatever substances our son shall give in the Gaṅgā,
all of them will indeed become inexhaustible for us.” / And the ancestors residing in hell, accompanied by all kinds of suffering,
say, upon seeing their son going to the bank of the Jāhnavī: / “Whatever sins were committed that caused suffering in hell,
all of them will go to destruction by the grace of our son. / Delivered from the hellish torments that were so intolerable,
we shall then, by the son’s grace, attain the supreme state.” / The mortal who, having undertaken the pilgrimage, turns back to his home out of delusion,
all his ancestors go away disappointed, just as they came. / Meat and sexual intercourse, a litter, a horse, and likewise an elephant,
shoes, and an umbrella—these one should avoid on pilgrimages to the Gaṅgā. / He does not regard the suffering born of the fatigue of the journey as difficult to bear;
and he should not remember the pleasure of his lotus-like home while bathing in the Gaṅgā. / Speaking falsehood and company with heretics,
eating twice, and quarreling—these one should avoid on pilgrimages to the Gaṅgā. / Slander of others, greed, pride, anger, and envy,
excessive laughter, and grief—these one should avoid on pilgrimages to the Gaṅgā. / Lying on the ground, he should imagine himself sleeping on a couch.
A person should utter the auspicious names of the Gaṅgā while walking on the road. / Proclaiming on the road the glorification of goddess Jāhnavī, which destroys all sin,
and which brings happiness and gives liberation, he travels: / “O goddess Gaṅgā, mother of the universe, grant me your sight!”
With these gentle words he should dispel his fatigue. / But he who says: “Alas, how was home abandoned, or how did I arrive [here]
with so much toil?”—his fruit is surely not complete. / “Where is my bed? Where is my wife? And where is the house of my friend?
I sleep on the ground in the wilderness! Or why did I come? / And what will become of the money, grain, and other goods in my home?
In how many days shall I go home again?” / The men who travel on the road troubled by such anxieties—
their fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā, O twice-born, will not be complete. / “O Gaṅgā, in order to reach your bank, this journey has been undertaken to you;
may I attain unimpeded success through your grace, O best of rivers!” / Having pronounced this mantra, especially at the time of departure,
he should go from his house joyful, along with Vaiṣṇavas, O Jaimini. / One should not go too swiftly, nor should one go very slowly;
on pilgrimages to the Gaṅgā, the wise should perform no other business. / But he who conducts business, such as trade, on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
or at Prayāga, half of his merit is lost. / “Whatever sin has been acquired through birth after birth, whether little or much,
it will all go to destruction through the grace of the goddess Gaṅgā.” / Having said this, supremely joyful, the wise man should proceed to the bank of the Gaṅgā;
and seeing mother Gaṅgā, he should utter this mantra: / “Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life has become truly lived,
since with my own eyes I have beheld you, who are the very embodiment of Brahman! / O goddess, simply by the sight of you, of me, a great sinner,
the sin arisen through ten million births has been destroyed!” / Having said this and prostrated his whole body on the surface of the earth,
he should bow down to the goddess Jāhnavī, endowed with a devotional disposition. / Then, near the current, with folded hands, O best of the twice-born,
delighted, he should recite this mantra with a devotional disposition: / “O goddess Gaṅgā, upholder of the world, that I touch your water with my feet—
being gracious, you ought to forgive this offense of mine! / Your water, O auspicious one, is the stairway for ascending to heaven;
therefore I touch it with my feet. O goddess Gaṅgā, homage, homage to you!” / Then, having placed the water of the Gaṅgā on his head with devotion,
the wise man should enter the current to bathe, chanting “Gaṅgā!” / “With your mud, very soothing and destroying all sins,
my body is smeared; O mother, remove my sin!” / His limbs smeared with the mud of the Gaṅgā, chanting “Gaṅgā! Gaṅgā!”
he should perform his bath in the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of all impurities. / Then again, having taken clay with the previously stated mantra,
and having taken clay again with the mantra that is about to be spoken, / he should perform his bath with devotion according to the mantra to be spoken:
“O Gaṅgā, whose form is Brahman, a bath is being performed by me / in your spotless water; grant the fruit as stated!”
Then, according to his desire, O brahmin, the wise man should take a bath / in the Gaṅgā, the mother of the world, remembering Gaṅgā-Nārāyaṇa.
Having thus bathed in the Gaṅgā, he should wipe his body with a cloth. / One should not cast the water from one's worn clothes into the current of the Gaṅgā.
The wise person should not clean his teeth within the belly of the Gaṅgā. / If he should do so out of delusion, he will not obtain the merit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Having performed the cleaning with a tooth-stick and the like elsewhere in the morning, / and having discarded the night-garment, he should perform his bath in the Gaṅgā.
He who should perform a bath in the Gaṅgā without having gone to the latrine, / he too will certainly not obtain the complete fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.

And having bathed, the wise man should apply the clay-mark of the Gaṅgā to the various places [on his body]. / Then, with a steady mind, he should perform the ancestral oblations and other rites according to rule.
He who performs the ancestral oblations with the waters of the Gaṅgā, / his ancestors are satisfied for a hundred million years.
He who performs an ancestral śrāddha in the Gaṅgā, O best of the twice-born, / his ancestors dwell contented in the abode of the thirty [gods].
Having completed the bath rites, having fasted at the Gaṅgā, / giving gifts, worshipping the gods, and other rites— / whatever is done at the Gaṅgā has no destruction.
Having completed the bath rites, having fasted at the Gaṅgā, / and having performed the five great sacrifices, he should perform the worship of the Gaṅgā.
The wise man should bathe the image of the goddess Gaṅgā and the image of Śrī Viṣṇu / with celestial coconut waters out of devotion.
In the absence of an image of the Jāhnavī, he should cast coconut waters / into the water of the Jāhnavī, remembering the Jāhnavī in his heart,
with divine perfumes and lamps blazing full of ghee, / with fragrant incenses, and with various enchanting flowers.
With various well-ripened fruits, excellent food offerings, / foot-water, respectful offerings, sipping-water, and betel leaves with acacia catechu,
and with other special presents according to one's own devotion, / with various hymns and offerings of food, one should worship the Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu.
Then, having worshipped the goddess and Viṣṇu, the supreme Lord, / the wise person should perform circumambulations with devotion three times.
“Now, having remained without food, on the next day, O best of rivers, / I shall eat, O daughter of Jahnu; be my refuge, O sinless one.”
Having thus formed his resolve in action, mind, and speech, the wise man, / having overcome sleep, greatly rejoiced, should keep vigil during the night.
And in case of incapacity, O best of twice-born, he may take only fruit as food below [the normal fast]; / he should not eat any grain, nor should he indeed take a full meal.
In the morning, having worshipped the Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu once again, O Jaimini, / he should give a priestly gift to a brāhmaṇa according to his means,
“May the worship and the vigil that were performed before you / all be free of fault through your grace, O best of rivers!”
Having spoken thus and bowed to her, the twice-born, having performed his daily duties, / should then himself carry out the breaking of the fast together with his kinsmen.
Whoever performs such a fast at the sacred ford on the bank of the Jāhnavī— / listen to the fruit of his merit as I describe it, dear child.
Liberated from the sins accumulated across other lifetimes, assuming the form of Viṣṇu, / he reaches the city of Viṣṇu and rejoices with Viṣṇu.
Remaining in Viṣṇu's city for thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of kalpas, / he enjoys all happiness that is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Then, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, he goes to Brahmā's world; / in Brahmā's world he enjoys happiness that is hard to attain even for the gods.
Having dwelt for so long in Brahmā's world, after the destruction of Brahmā, / he would then go to Mahādeva, mounting a splendid chariot.
There he enjoys various kinds of happiness, exceedingly hard to attain; / he obtains the status of a Gaṇa—what need of many words?
Having stayed in Śiva's city for so long, that meritorious man / would then go to Indra's world as a second Vāsava.
He would then dwell on the same throne with that virtuous soul; / having enjoyed all desires there for up to a hundred crores of kalpas,
he would then go to Sūrya's world as a second moon; / having enjoyed nectars there for a long time in the presence of the moon,
having returned again to the earth, he becomes a universal monarch, / having long protected the earth and having conquered all enemies.
And at the end of his life, he attains a peaceful death in the Gaṅgā; / then, possessing exceedingly great fame, having mounted an aerial chariot,
he goes to the city of the Blessed One, hard to attain even by deities; / having enjoyed all pleasures there for four manvantaras,
having attained supreme knowledge, he attains liberation, hard to obtain. / If by chance someone's demise should occur on the road
during a pilgrimage to the bank of the Jāhnavī, he too goes to the supreme abode, without doubt. / There was a king named Satyadharma, righteous and sweet-spoken,
at the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages upon the circle of the earth. / That king had a chief queen named Vijayā,
beautiful, endowed with good conduct, devoted to serving her husband. / Having enjoyed this earth for seven thousand years,
once, his time having come, he passed away along with his wife. / Then, bound by Yama's soldiers, that fearful couple,
went to Yama's abode along a misery-granting path. / Having seen the two, Dharmarāja spoke to Citragupta:
“O Citragupta, examine all the deeds of these two.” / Commanded by him, Citragupta, O Jaimini,
examined the deeds of the two from the beginning and, with joined palms, spoke: / Citragupta said: “Hear all the deeds of these two, O king; I shall tell them:
the good or evil deed that was done by these two on earth. / I shall mention a certain unjust deed of his; hear that from me.
Once, terrified by tigers, a certain deer, O Lord, / came from the forest to his assembly to protect its life.
Beholding it approaching, this king, feeling curiosity, / rose up himself and quickly struck the deer with a sword.
The king struck down this deer even though it had approached for refuge; / therefore this king, together with his wife, must be punished by you, O Lord.
For as many hairs as were present on its body, / for thousands of manvantaras and hundreds of manvantaras,
along with crores and crores of his lineage, he would be a denizen of hell, no doubt. / Whoever protects one who comes for refuge, even with his life or his wealth—
whoever that wise man is, listen to his merit: / freed from all sins, even those beginning with the murder of a brāhmaṇa,
at the end of his life he goes to liberation, hard to attain even for yogins.” / Then, by Yama's command, that king, along with his wife,
was placed by the messengers in the dreadful Sword-Leaved Forest, causing intense misery. / Because the leaves of those trees are like swords,
the wise call it the Sword-Leaved Forest. / Having stayed in the sword-leaved woods for hundreds of crores of yugas,
together with his wife he then went to the hell named Vyāghrabhakṣya. / One who enters that hell, filled with all kinds of distress,
becomes food for a tiger; therefore it is remembered as Vyāghrabhakṣya. / Having stayed there for thousands of crores of yugas, that king,
at the end of his sins, was born on earth along with his wife, having entered the womb of a frog. / Remembering their past births, the two of them, female frog and male frog, were very miserable.
Eating insects continually, they remained on a riverbank. / Then, once, along that path, humans, having reached an auspicious day,
were going to the bank of the Jāhnavī; the two frogs saw them, O twice-born. / The male frog said: “O frog, because of all the sinful deeds done by me out of delusion,
even today, because of that deed, misery does not leave the two of us. / Having abandoned their body in the Gaṅgā, even sinners are liberated;
even so, how are we to experience such suffering? / I desire now to abandon this body in the Gaṅgā.
Tell me, my beloved, what plan [to follow], wishing as I do to cross the ocean of sorrow.” / Having heard his words, the female frog spoke with humility.
The female frog said: “Suffering cannot be endured, O lord; do this quickly!” / Then that couple, O brāhmaṇa, remembering the auspicious Gaṅgā,
suddenly set out on the journey to death, full of joy. / Then, as they were going along the path, starved for a long time,
a venomous, dreadful black serpent, an evil-doer, saw them. / The black serpent said: “O two sinful frogs! Since your time has arrived,
now you two must certainly be eaten by me who am hungry.” / Then that couple, partners in sorrow, deeply terrified,
spoke these words with devotion to the black serpent standing before them: / “O serpent, there is not even the slightest fear of death in our hearts.
Formerly I was a king on earth named Satyadharma, / and this wife of mine was queen named Vijayā.
Out of delusion, one who had come for refuge was destroyed by me, an evil-souled person; / by that very deed, sorrow was suffered for a long time in Yama's abode.
To experience the remainder of my past action, together with my wife, / I have entered the womb of a frog because of sin; done deeds do not release one.
Truly, we two wish to go to the supreme abode, O serpent; / we are going to the bank of the Jāhnavī in order to abandon our bodies.
Abandon this lack of discrimination, O snake, which causes the afflictions of hell! / How much pleasure will there be for you from devouring both of us?
Viṣṇu is in our hearts, and Hari is in your heart as well; / therefore, what enmity can there be with you, O serpent?
Violence to living beings should never be done by discerning people; / and even if it is done, the Ordainer Himself arranges that violence [upon the perpetrator].
Lifespan, sons, wives, riches, and fame— / giving violence to human beings, wicked fate itself would take [these] away.
What use are recitations, what use are austerities, what use are gifts, or what use are sacrifices, / for him in whose heart the two syllables “violence” [hiṃ-sā] always reside?
Whatever mortal harms living beings, he harms Hari; / the Lord, husband of Kamalā, abides in the body of all living beings.
Having created Himself in many forms, the Lord, the source of beings, / plays by Himself like a child in the playhouse of saṃsāra.
For the body of an embodied being is the abode of the Supreme Self; / the Supreme Self Himself is Viṣṇu; therefore one should abandon violence.
Self-gratification is arranged through the destruction of another's life.
For a moment there is gratification for oneself, but total loss of life for another; / this conduct of people on earth is exceedingly astonishing!
They cause their own satisfaction by killing another with great effort; / a wise man never lacks self-knowledge.
“I am Viṣṇu, and that one is Viṣṇu”—thus one should contemplate in mind; / he who is sorrowful at another's sorrow, and happy at another's prosperity,
he is to be recognized in this world as Hari Himself in person. / Cursed be that pleasure of men whose minds are deluded by infatuation,
which arises through inflicting violence upon another, O serpent! / Whatever pleasures or sorrows are given to a creature,
human beings indeed receive those very same things on earth without delay. / Therefore, abandon violence, O serpent, and be happy.

When you are pleased, we two shall go to the farther shore of the great ocean of sorrow.
The snake said: / If there were indeed supreme sin in harming another for me,
then why, alas, were food and eater created by the Creator? / Violence to another must not be done—this has been spoken truly by you.
However, violence is not conceived in all edible things. / Nārāyaṇa is the universal form—this is true, no doubt;
He Himself indeed created [the world] conjoined with food and eater. / He Himself creates Himself, and He Himself protects Himself;
He Himself eats Himself; such is the creation of Hari. / Am I able to slay you two? The Ordainer Himself has the form of Time;
Hari Himself sent me right now for this work. / The God who created you two, and who always protects you two,

that very same one, having the form of Time, slays [you] today, making me the instrument.
Vyāsa said: / Then those two, husband and wife, were devoured by that serpent,
murmuring “Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā!” on the path out of great hunger. / In the journey to the bank of the Jāhnavī, at every step, these two people
attained the great fruit of the sacrifices called horse sacrifice. / Therefore, these two high-souled ones possess [the merit of] many horse sacrifices.
“There is no equal to these two; I am Indra [only because of a hundred sacrifices]”; / Purandara, taking hold of another [chariot] solely in his own official capacity,
came on foot, with offering in hand, surrounded by the gods. / Then Rambhā, Urvaśī, and other beauties, delighted,
spoke to one another, proud of their own youth: / “This foremost of virtuous souls is a connoisseur and exceedingly handsome;
now that he has arrived, I will bring him under my control through my services.” / One woman said to another: “I know every single art,
therefore I shall be the beloved of this king.” / One woman said to another: “Even Śakra is under my control;
what wonder is there that this king will become compliant [to me]?”
“This one is my husband, and he is my protector; this one is my master, and he is my lord!” / Thus indeed, with supreme delights, spoke all the women, connoisseurs of all fine virtues.
Hearing their varied talk, O brāhmaṇa, a certain virtuous, discerning woman said: / “The king himself enjoys whichever woman pleases him; why do you women quarrel?”
Then all those beauties, abandoning the quarrel, O twice-born one, / came with zeal in their hearts, adorned with all ornaments.
Then they worshiped that best of kings, who was accompanied by his wife and freed from sin, / with foot-water and other offerings; Purandara spoke [to him]:
He seated him along with his wife in the Puṣpaka chariot. / With the sounds of kettle-drums, mṛdaṅgas, madhurīs, ḍiṇḍimas, and ānakas,
and with the tinkling of hand-bracelets and the sounds of clapping, / and with the gods' cries of victory, heaven became full of sound.
Fanned by breezes from white cawries in the lovely hands of heavenly women, / mounted upon the chariot, he went to heaven with his wife.
Then Śakra himself, fearing the destruction of his own fortune, / gave half of his own seat to that king Satyadharma.
Dwelling always on the same seat with Śakra, that king / exercised kingship in heaven through the compassion of Keśava.
Having enjoyed all happiness in heaven for tens of millions of yugas, / he mounted a chariot and went to Vaikuṇṭha by the command of the Lord.
Having enjoyed every delight that is pleasing to the mind there for a manvantara, / and having attained supreme knowledge, he attained liberation together with his wife.
For one who abandons the body on the road during the journey to the bank of the Jāhnavī, / such is the fruit; everything has been proclaimed by me, O brāhmaṇa.
Regarding going to the bank of the Jāhnavī, no restriction of time has been stated / by the sages who perceive reality, nor by the great sages beginning with Nārada.
Whenever, O best of the twice-born, a person performs a bath in the Gaṅgā, / then, indeed, a human being unfailingly obtains imperishable merit.
The Gaṅgā destroys all sins—this is certain; / but if one should commit sin again and again, the Gaṅgā does not purify him.
Abandoning sinful intent, take a bath in the Gaṅgā, the mother of the world, / O people, if you desire a good destination!
The merit that human beings obtain from bathing in the Gaṅgā, O twice-born one— / by what actions, exceedingly hard to perform, can that merit be obtained, O brāhmaṇa?
It is possible to count torrential downpours and the dust particles of the earth, / but the virtues of the Bhāgīrathī cannot be spoken by anyone, O twice-born one.
Having deliberated upon all the scriptures belonging to you, it is declared by me: / having bathed even once in the waters of the Gaṅgā, a human being attains liberation.

Even one who bathes in well-water, contemplating the Gaṅgā—the master of the gods, the destroyer of the mass of all afflictions, sorrows, sins, and terrors— / he too, freed from the mass of all sins such as killing cows and brāhmaṇas, would go to the city of Viṣṇu which bestows all happiness, by the grace of the Gaṅgā, O twice-born one.

7.10.m: Jaimini said: / This glorification of the Gaṅgā has been heard by me through your grace; / now I wish to hear the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu, O guru.

Vyāsa said:
Listen, dear child, to the supreme fruit of worshiping the husband of Lakṣmī, / having heard which, all mortals attain supreme knowledge.
O brāhmaṇa, among the twelve months beginning with Māgha, hear those rites / by which the eternal [Lord] is to be worshiped; I shall speak of them.
When the auspicious month of Māgha arrives, the best of all months, / the excellent Vaiṣṇava must renounce meat and sexual intercourse.
He should always bathe at dawn, and avoid oils as well; / he should give up eating twice [a day] and eating another’s food in the month of Māgha.
Wearing white garments at dawn, having performed the five great sacrifices, / a man with a steady mind should indeed begin the worship of Viṣṇu.
He should bathe the imperishable Viṣṇu with pure, slightly warm water, / and smear the limbs of Viṣṇu with very fine sandal-paste.
He should worship the Lord of the universe, the God of gods, who bears the discus; / he should clean the vessels and leave them free of water.
Having bathed the Lord of the world with slightly warm water, / his body should be carefully wiped with a divine cloth.
If one bathes Keśava with slightly warm waters / in the month of Māgha, O best of the twice-born, I shall state his reward:
Freed from all sins accumulated across many births, / he enjoys all happiness in this world, and in the end goes to the abode of Hari.
Having carefully washed the vessels and made them pure with water, / heed the merit of him who worships the Lord of the world:
Having enjoyed all desires in this world, free from all diseases, / in the end he remains in the abode of Keśava for thousands of yugas.
At dawn and at dusk, before the discus-bearing Lord, / a Vaiṣṇava person should place a blazing, smokeless fire.
To ward off the cold in Māgha, a Vaiṣṇava should kindle a fire / before Viṣṇu in the evening and in the morning. Hear the reward of that:
Having enjoyed all desires here, accompanied by sons and grandsons, / in the end he goes to the city of Viṣṇu, difficult even for the gods to attain.
Viṣṇu is just like one's own self; there is no doubt in this. / When Keśava, the God of gods, is sleeping upon his couch,
just as a mortal wards off cold for himself, / what would the supreme god Viṣṇu, well-pleased, not grant to him / who bathes Janārdana with milk in the month of Māgha?
so should he dispel the cold for the discus-bearer with a divine cloth.
He who bathes the four-armed [Lord] with coconut-water and milk / and worships him even once in Māgha, I will proclaim his reward:
Having delivered ten million ancestors sinking in the ocean of hell, / which is difficult to cross because of one’s own deeds, he goes to the realm of the discus-bearer.
In the month of Māgha, on the bright fifth day, O best of the twice-born, / and on the eleventh and the fifteenth, worship of Hari is especially [meritorious].
Day after day in the month of Māgha, milk-rice along with incense / should be offered to the God of gods, who holds the lotus, the enemy of Mura.
To him who offers milk-rice accompanied by incense to the discus-bearer in Māgha, / I declare the meritorious fruit; hear, O Vaiṣṇava Jaimini!
In the end, having gone to the city of Viṣṇu for four manvantaras, / he enjoys delightful pleasures by the grace of the discus-bearing Lord.
Having returned to the earth, he becomes a universal emperor; / having enjoyed pleasure for a very long time, upon death he goes to the abode of Hari.
Or on the fifth, on the seventh, and on the eleventh, O Jaimini, / an incapable Vaiṣṇava may offer rice-pudding to the enemy of Mura.
More especially during the bright fortnight than the dark fortnight, O best of the twice-born, / one should offer food to the enemy of Mura on these lunar days in the bright fortnight.
He who, even for a single day in Māgha, offers milk-rice with cakes / to Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the Daityas—Hari is not difficult for him to attain.
Whatever is offered in the month of Māgha for the pleasure of the twice-born / becomes imperishable for a man; there is no doubt about this.
Action performed in the month of Māgha, whether good or indeed evil, / has no destruction, O brāhmaṇa, even in hundreds of manvantaras.
He who worships the Lord of Kamalā in Māgha with a campaka flower, / freed from all sins, goes to the supreme abode.
For as many golden flowers as are given to the discus-bearing Lord, / for that many thousands of yugas does one dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.
The reward that comes from giving gold equal [in weight] to Mount Meru, / that reward is attained by worshiping Hari with a single golden flower.
A golden flower, O best of brāhmaṇas, is always dear to Keśava; / especially in the month of Māgha, it is pure and dear to Keśava.
He by whom Hari is not worshiped with divine golden flowers / shall be bereft of jewels, gold, and the like, birth after birth.
I will tell in detail the fruit of the campaka flower; / hear, O best of the twice-born, this supreme legendary history.
There was a king named Suvarṇa, powerful and knowledgeable in all scriptures, / [renowned] throughout all Āryāvarta for the splendor of a brāhmaṇa.
Through royal splendor, learning, and youth, that ruler of the earth / became exceedingly intoxicated, O sage among brāhmaṇas, and was constantly devoted to sin.
Following the words of heretical ministers, even when they were blameless, O twice-born, / virtuous people were punished by that king out of greed for wealth.
Surrounded by singing, instrumental music, and the like, / he squandered all the wealth acquired unlawfully, devoid of sacrifices and charity.
He did not support his kinsmen, nor did he feed the gods and the twice-born, / nor did he satisfy supplicants, being always bewildered by sin.
Always intent on evil deeds, he never performed worship of guests; / and that king, an abode of sins, constantly went away from his temple.
The sins committed by that man—those of thoughtless persons— / would anyone be able to enumerate them even in a hundred years?
Once that protector of the earth, completely infatuated with desire, / went to a courtesan’s dwelling at midnight, his mind set on evil.
Then, seeing the ruler of the earth arriving, the woman named Ujjvalā / rose up quickly on the bed and bowed to his feet.
Having washed his pair of feet with water from a pitcher, / she embraced that king with her arms and seated him upon the couch.
Drenched by streams of the nectar of her love, that lord of the earth / sat upon that bed with her, filled with eagerness.
Then that courtesan, smiling in her prime of youth, / lovingly gave him campaka flowers herself to the ruler of the earth.
From the flower garland, a single flower fell from the king's hand / onto the surface of the earth, its fragrance pervading all directions.
Seeing that fallen flower, the king, out of great agitation, / said, 'Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa,' preceded by the syllable Oṃ.
Through the utterance of the word 'To Nārāyaṇa' / and through offering the golden flower, all the sins of that king were destroyed.
Then all the villagers, coming together at an invincible hour, / killed him in that very night while he was inside the courtesan's house.
Then, to carry off that king, the foremost of all sinners, / the son of Vivasvat, exceedingly enraged, sent his servants.
Commanded by him, the messengers, holding nooses and clubs in their hands, / arrived with great speed, their eyes red with anger.
The messengers of Yama made an effort to lead him to their own realm; / then the servants of Nārāyaṇa, bearing conch, discus, and mace,
Mounted on Garuḍa, they arrived to lead that ruler of the earth away. / Seeing that king restrained in fetters, Viṣṇu's attendants,
Mighty in strength, struck Yama's messengers with discs and maces. / Placing him on a celestial chariot, they blew their peerless conches.
Mounted likewise on the chariot, adorned with a garland of tulasī, / Wearing yellow silk garments and embellished with golden ornaments,
Praised by hosts of sages who had mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, / Surrounded by Viṣṇu's messengers, he went to Hari's world.
Then Viṣṇu himself arose, and with his four long arms / Embraced that king, O best of the twice-born, and spoke:
The Blessed Lord said: / Speak of your welfare, O king, best among all virtuous souls! / What wish of yours is to be fulfilled? Command it now!
He who says even once, “Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa,” / Must always be protected by me; he is my brother, he is my father.
Whatever mortal at any time remembers my name, “Nārāyaṇa,” / I fulfill all his desires, as a son does for his father.
You are my devotee, O best of kings; therefore, disclose your marvelous / Desire, my friend! What may I give you now?
The king said: / Everything has indeed been granted by you, O ocean of mercy, without a doubt! / Even sinner that I was, I have attained your abode, so difficult to reach.
Pleased with these words of his, the lord of Kamalā / Affectionately seated the ruler of the earth; listen to that:
Then, with golden ornaments fashioned by Viśvakarman, / The compassionate one personally arranged an adornment for him.
Then, with various divine eatables exceedingly hard to obtain, / That king was gratified by Viṣṇu, who is exceedingly forbearing.
In this way, that king remained daily in Viṣṇu's abode / For a thousand manvantaras and nine hundred years.
That king, intent on dharma, protected his subjects; / He constantly worshipped Hari with supreme devotion,
With lovely campaka flowers and various offerings of food. / At the end of his lifespan, that ruler of the earth met his death in the water of the Jāhnavī,
And attained liberation through the grace of the one who bears the disc in his hand. / Vyāsa said: / O brahmin, the power of the campaka flower has thus been proclaimed.
By worshipping Hari with campakas, even sinful people become liberated. / When the Blessed Lord Hari is worshipped with a blossoming campaka flower,
He soon grants the supreme abode, O brahmin-sage! / Those who worship the Supreme Self, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
They too, freed from all sins, go to the supreme abode.
When Hari is pleased, no one remains a sinner, since even that king who had committed sins / Attained liberation through Murāri's mercy, crossing over this deep cosmic ocean.
A mortal who worships Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes are wide as lotus petals, / With divine, fragrant golden blossoms with devotion and supreme reverence, leaves behind sin and attains that [abode].

7.11.m: Vyāsa said: / According to what rite Hari must always be worshipped, O Jaimini, / That I shall tell you, O brahmin-sage; listen attentively, dear child.
Rising from bed at dawn, taking a vessel of water, / The wise man should go outside, having covered his head with a cloth.
There, facing the northern direction, silent, having placed his sacred thread / Over his ears, seated, the wise man should discharge feces and urine.
In a temple of a deity, on a path, in cowpens, and in courtyards, / On a public street, in ploughed land, at the root of darbha grass, and in a front yard,
On the bank of a river, at the foot of a sacred fig tree, and likewise in a forest, / And in the beds of tanks and wells, one should not discharge feces or urine.
The sun, the moon, brahmins, cows, and the ten directions— / While discharging feces and urine, the wise man does not look at these.
Earth dug up by mice and the like, situated inside a hole, / And ploughed by a plowshare—one must never take this for the purpose of purification.
Fetching water from a water-source, the discerning man should perform purification; / A wise man does not perform purification having placed his foot in the water.
Facing south at night, the wise man should attend to the bodily necessity; / Having covered his head with a cloth, he should then perform purification.
One application of clay is to be given to the penis, and three to the anus; / Seven to the left hand, and ten to both hands by the wise.
Six applications of clay are to be given to the feet by the discerning. / Having performed the purification rites, the wise man should clean his teeth
And scrape his tongue with tooth-cloths and the like. / Having turned facing south, or likewise facing west,
One should not clean one's teeth; if one does, one will go to hell. / With the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, O twice-born,
One should clean one's teeth; never with the forefinger. / From the aśvattha, the banyan tree, the dhātrī, or the kaithika, the wise man
Should not make a tooth-cleaning twig, nor likewise from the trees sacred to Indra and the gods; / The daily fruit of his rites is entirely destroyed.
He who cleans his teeth at the time of bathing, O Jaimini— / His ancestors, the gods, and the divine sages depart hopeless.
He who cleans his teeth at midday or in the afternoon— / The deities do not accept his worship, nor the ancestors his water.
He who cleans his teeth in a lotus-pond at the time of bathing / Is to be known as an outcaste until he sees the Gaṅgā.
He who cleans his teeth after the venerable sun has arisen— / Consuming that tooth-stick, his ancestors depart full of sorrow.
On a fast day, O brahmin, and on the day of an ancestral rite, / A man who cleans his teeth [with a stick] does not attain that fruit.
In the morning, the wise man should clean his teeth and tongue with a cloth; / He should rinse twelve times with water, O chief of brahmins.
On a fast day and an ancestral rite, performing the cleaning of teeth / In accordance with this rule, O Jaimini, a mortal obtains the full fruit.
Having performed the evacuation in accordance with this rule, the farsighted man / Should then go to his house and cast off his night-garment.
Then, seated at the door of the shrine, pure, the wise man / Should remember God Nārāyaṇa, the infinite, the supreme lord:
“O Rāma! O dark-bodied Viṣṇu! O Nārāyaṇa full of compassion! / O Janārdana! O abode of the universe! Remove my sin, O Keśava!
O wearer of yellow garments! O Ananta! O Padmanābha! O embodiment of the world! / O Vāmana! O Lord of the bowed! O all-pervading one, be my refuge!
O Dāmodara! O best of the Yadus! O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! O ocean of mercy! / O lotus-eyed one! O lord of gods! O Vāsudeva, show compassion!
O one whose emblem is Garuḍa! O Govinda! O supporter of the universe! O bearer of the mace! / O conch-handed one! O disc-handed one! O lotus-handed one! Remove my distress!
O delight of Lakṣmī! O Vaikuṇṭha! O Hṛṣīkeśa! O best of the gods! / O Puruṣottama! O enemy of Kaṃsa! O enemy of Kaiṭabha! Dispel my fear!
O lord of Śrī! O Śrīdhara! O all-pervading one! O bestower of prosperity! O causer of prosperity! O Mādhava! / O supreme Brahman! O supreme abode! Be my refuge, O imperishable one!”
Having thus performed the remembrance of glorious Viṣṇu, O best of the twice-born, the wise man, / Entering into his dwelling with folded hands, speaks thus:
“O Lord! O lord of Śrī! O Kṛṣṇa! O joy of Devakī! O master! / Relinquish sleep, O Jagannātha! The time of morning has come!”
Then, having cast off sleep, the wise man should contemplate in his mind / the son of Devakī accompanied by Lakṣmī as if risen upon His couch.
Then the Vaiṣṇava should offer to Kṛṣṇa a covered, divine vessel / filled with water for rinsing His mouth.
Just as servants serve their master for livelihood, / even so the wise serve the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, he who serves the Lord of the universe in the form of a servant, / O brahmin sage, his desire is accomplished without delay.
Just as attendants perform service to their master with reverence, / so the wise always serve Lord Hari.
If a man worships Viṣṇu according to his own whims, devoid of reverence, / he is a bad servant, and it will not bear fruit, O brahmin.
Therefore, O best of brahmins, service to the Lord of Kamalā / must always be performed with promptness by a man desiring absolute liberation.
The Vaiṣṇava person should remove from Hari's body in the morning / the withered flower offerings, the night garments, and the stale fragrance.
Then he himself should sweep that temple of the deity; / the wise man should gradually cleanse it with a broom.
As many particles of dust as go out from that abode, / for so many hundreds of manvantaras a person will dwell in Viṣṇu's house.
Even a slayer of a brahmin who sweeps Hari's house / goes to the supreme abode; what need of many words?
Likewise, O brahmin, the wise man should smear that house of Viṣṇu / with moist cow dung, remembering Lord Nārāyaṇa.
He who smears the temple of Keśava, / of his merit I shall speak in brief; listen, O Jaimini.
As many specks of dust as are destroyed there, O best of brahmins, / for so many thousands of kalpas he will dwell happy in Viṣṇu's house.
A person having swept and smeared Viṣṇu's house / attains the supreme abode; what need to speak of the fruit of worshipping the Lord?
When, due to an obstacle from the king or deity, he is unable to do so himself, / he should employ his lawful wife in Viṣṇu's house.
Or he should appoint in the temple of the deity / his own devoted, virtuous son, or his brother, or his sister.
He himself should wash the articles for Hari's worship with great care / seven times with pure water, or three times.
Copper vessels are purified with acid, bell-metal vessels with ashes, / and iron vessels with fire; of this there is no doubt.
A wealthy person who bathes Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe, / with water kept in an iron vessel—with him Keśava is not pleased.
Or if it happens out of ignorance, he is purified by bathing in the Gaṅgā; / in prosperity, O best of brahmins, the rule must always be observed.
In misfortune there is no strict rule: such is the determination in the scriptures. / When a conch, carefully washed, touches the ground again,
then, O chief of brahmins, that conch is not purified even by being washed a hundred times. / Having thus carefully washed the worship materials of the wielder of the discus,
and taking the materials for bathing, he should go to a pond to bathe. / He who returns home without having performed the rites of bathing,
on that day the multitude of his ancestors does not obtain water offerings. / If one creates an obstacle for a person going to bathe or eat,
he who does so out of delusion, O best of brahmins, surely goes to hell. / He who, having gone to a pond to bathe, passes feces and urine,
his ancestors will consume feces and urine, of this there is no doubt. / Then, having performed bathing and water offerings according to the rule,
the wise man should return to his own house, remembering Nārāyaṇa. / And then in the courtyard, O brahmin, having washed both feet,
the pure one, best of brahmins, should enter the sanctuary of the deity. / The person who enters the abode with unwashed feet,
his merit acquired over a year is destroyed that very moment. / Having bathed and arrived in the courtyard, the discerning man,
having washed both feet, should therefore enter the house of the deity. / Having sat down, the wise man, with the left hand,
should carefully wash both feet, O brahmin, and then both hands; / foot by foot, O chief of brahmins, and also with the right hand.
And the foolish person who washes them [improperly], Lakṣmī surely abandons him. / Then, being seated, the intelligent man should begin the worship of Keśava,
becoming single-minded, which grants the fruits of all desires. / On a pure seat of deer skin, or on a seat of tiger skin,
or on a mere cloth seat, and likewise on a seat made of kuśa grass, / or seated on a flower seat, he should worship the Lord of Kamalā.
A learned brahmin should not perform the worship of Viṣṇu on a wooden seat. / 'You are held by Viṣṇu, O Earth, and all the worlds are held by you;
therefore, O all-bearing one, give me an excellent place to sit.' / Having spoken thus and spread the seat, the worshipper of Nārāyaṇa should sit down.
Facing south, one should not perform the worship of Viṣṇu. / Having placed in a conch water purified with mantras and fragrant,
he should bathe the beloved of Kamalā, the Lord together with Kamalā. / He who bathes the Lord, Janārdana, with a conch,
I shall tell the fruit thereof; listen, O Jaimini, chief of brahmins. / Freed from sins such as slaying a brahmin, a cow, a woman, or an embryo, and drinking liquor,
he goes to Vaikuṇṭha and truly enjoys every happiness. / If a human being, looking upon Hṛṣīkeśa, worships Him, O brahmin,
he quickly attains that very thing by the grace of the Lord of Kamalā. / In the absence of a conch, however, O chief of brahmins, the wise man,
having placed fragrant water and tulasī in a vessel, should bathe Keśava. / Then, having bathed the God and placed Him on an excellent seat,
he should anoint all His limbs with fragrant sandalpaste, / and protect the body of the wielder of the discus with the paste of tulasī wood.

The person who does so—Hari is always pleased with him.
'This garland of tulasī leaves, bestowing the joy of its own fragrance,

is given to you, O Lord of the Universe; be well pleased forever.'
With this mantra, O best of Brahmins, when Mahāviṣṇu is adorned

with a garland of tulasī leaves, what will he not give when pleased?
Then, the recitation of svastivācana should be performed with Vedic mantras.

And the binding of the directions should be performed by the wise with Puranic mantras:
'May Kṛṣṇa protect in the east; may the son of Devakī [protect] in the south-east;

may the enemy of the Daityas protect in the south; may Madhusūdana [protect] in the south-west;
may the glorious one protect in the intermediate directions; and may the Lord, the bearer of Śrī, protect above;

may the Self of the Universe, merciful in the form of a tortoise, protect below.
Whatever obstacle-makers may arise at the time of worship,

may they all go far away, struck down by the weapon of Hari's name.'
Having thus performed the binding of the directions, then, bowed down with joined palms,

he makes a firm resolve with the mantra about to be spoken:
'O God of gods, O Janārdana, bring this worship begun by me

to fulfillment without obstacles; be pleased, O Supreme Lord.'
Then, having made the resolve, the Vaiṣṇava who knows all reality,

having performed the placement of the limbs and the rest, should meditate in his heart on Nārāyaṇa,
resembling a fresh raincloud, with eyes resembling white lotus flowers,

the god wearing yellow garments, with a smiling, charming face,
adorned with garlands of kadamba flowers, endowed with mighty arms,

wearing earrings, his crest bound with peacock feathers,
enchanting the ten directions with the sweet sound of his flute,

surrounded by cowherd women, abiding in beautiful Vṛndāvana.
Having thus meditated on the Lord of gods, Govinda, who grants all desires,

the Vaiṣṇava should then perform the invocation with a devotional disposition.
For Kṛṣṇa, who has been invoked, the bestower of the four aims of life,

the discerning one should present water for the feet, the respectful offering, and sipping water.
With tender tulasī leaves or delightful flowers, the wise one

should worship the Lord of all gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī:
'Salutations to the Fish, to the Tortoise, and to the Boar, salutations, salutations!

Salutations be to you, Hari! Salutations, salutations to Vāmana!
